Front: What does 'antiparallel' mean for DNA strands?
Back: The two strands run in opposite directions: one 5′→3′, the other 3′→5′.
A with T, G with C. In RNA, U replaces T, so A pairs with U.
Purines (two rings): A, G. Pyrimidines (one ring): C, T (U in RNA).
5′-TTCAGTCAT-3′ (complement each base, then reverse so it reads 5′→3′).

Front: Which strand does the reference genome FASTA store?
Back: Only the forward (+) strand of each chromosome; the − strand is implied as its reverse complement.
The read aligned to the reverse strand; SEQ and QUAL are stored reverse-complemented to match the + strand.

Front: Why do strand-bias filters exist (e.g. in FilterMutectCalls)?
Back: True variants are usually supported by reads from both orientations; artifacts often appear on only one.
A region of DNA transcribed into a functional RNA; for protein-coding genes, that RNA is translated into protein.
Exons are kept in the mature mRNA (and can include UTRs); introns are transcribed but removed by splicing.
Coding sequence: the exonic bases from the start codon to the stop codon that encode the protein.
Untranslated regions of the mRNA: the 5′ UTR before the start codon and the 3′ UTR after the stop. They are exonic but not translated.

Front: Start codon and stop codons (DNA letters)?
Back: Start: ATG (Met). Stops: TAA, TAG, TGA.
RNA polymerase reads the template strand; the RNA matches the coding (sense) strand with U for T. Annotation and c. notation use the coding strand.
Introns almost always start with GT (splice donor, 5′ splice site) and end with AG (splice acceptor, 3′ splice site).

Front: How do spliced RNA-seq aligners represent an intron in a read?
Back: With the CIGAR operator N (skipped reference region), e.g. 50M2000N50M.
Most amino acids are encoded by more than one codon, often differing at the third position, so many third-position changes are synonymous.

Front: How many codons, sense codons and stops?
Back: 64 codons: 61 encode the 20 amino acids, 3 are stop codons.
One way of dividing a sequence into consecutive codons; each strand has 3, giving 6 in total.

Front: Which c. positions form codon n?
Back: c.(3n−2) to c.3n. Example: codon 12 = c.34–c.36.
The A of the ATG start codon in a specific transcript; c. counts only coding bases and skips introns.
BED is 0-based, half-open (positions count from 0; the end coordinate is not included); VCF and GTF are 1-based, inclusive. VCF POS = BED start + 1.

Front: KRAS G12D: c. and p. notation?
Back: c.35G>A, p.Gly12Asp (p.G12D): codon GGT→GAT. On GRCh38 it appears in the VCF as chr12:25245350 C>T (KRAS is on the − strand).

Front: Why does a − strand gene's VCF change look 'different' from the report?
Back: The VCF shows the + strand; the report uses the gene's coding strand, so bases are complemented and c. runs opposite to genomic coordinates.
One representative transcript per protein-coding gene, with identical RefSeq (NM_) and Ensembl (ENST) versions that align perfectly to GRCh38; the recommended default for clinical reporting.
Extra transcripts for genes where MANE Select alone cannot describe all known pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants.
~147 bp of DNA wrapped around an octamer of histone proteins; the basic unit of chromatin packaging.
Euchromatin: open, gene-rich, actively transcribed. Heterochromatin: compact, gene-poor, quiet; constitutive heterochromatin (e.g. centromeres) is repeat-rich.

Front: Why can't standard WGS detect MGMT promoter methylation?
Back: Methylation is an epigenetic mark on the DNA, not a change in sequence; WGS reads sequence only (bisulfite or methylation-aware methods are needed).

Front: What is a centromere and what is it made of?
Back: The chromosome constriction where sister chromatids join and spindle fibres attach; built from huge arrays of ~171 bp α-satellite repeats.
p = short arm, q = long arm, on either side of the centromere. Cytobands are named arm + region + band, e.g. 17p13.1 (TP53).

Front: Which is shorter, chr21 or chr22?
Back: chr21 (~46.7 Mb) is shorter than chr22 (~50.8 Mb); the numbering reflects historical size estimates.
Ongoing mis-segregation of chromosomes during division, giving cell-to-cell karyotype variation; common in solid tumours.

Front: What is whole-genome doubling and why does it matter for VAF?
Back: A tumour copies its entire genome once, so the baseline copy number becomes ~4 instead of 2, changing expected VAFs.
t(9;22)(q34;q11), fusing BCR (chr22) to ABL1 (chr9); the defining lesion of CML and the target of imatinib.
+7/−10: gain of chromosome 7 with loss of chromosome 10.
Gains of odd-numbered chromosomes (3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 19, 21); seen in about half of myeloma cases.
DNA polymerase can't fully copy linear chromosome ends, so telomeres shorten with each division until cells senesce or die.
~85–90% reactivate telomerase (TERT + TERC); ~10–15% use ALT (recombination-based), associated with ATRX/DAXX loss.
They create new ETS (GABP) transcription-factor binding sites that reactivate TERT — non-coding drivers of replicative immortality.

Front: TERT C228T: name origin and GRCh38 VCF appearance?
Back: Named after GRCh37 chr5:1,295,228; in GRCh38 it is chr5:1,295,113 and appears as G>A because TERT is on the − strand (c.-124C>T).
Short regions at the tips of X and Y with identical sequence; males are diploid there. GRCh38 analysis sets mask the chrY copies.
16,569 bp circular genome, 37 genes, maternally inherited, hundreds to thousands of copies per cell; GRCh38 chrM = rCRS.

Front: What are NUMTs and why do they matter?
Back: Nuclear insertions of mitochondrial DNA; they attract mis-mapped mtDNA reads and create false nuclear variant calls.
A block >1 kb duplicated elsewhere with >90% identity; ~5% of the genome; causes ambiguous mapping and MAPQ 0.
Processed: reverse-transcribed mRNA copy without introns (e.g. PTENP1). Unprocessed: copy made by genomic duplication (e.g. PMS2CL).

Front: Why is PMS2 hard to sequence?
Back: Its 3′ exons are nearly identical to the pseudogene PMS2CL, so short reads get MAPQ 0; labs confirm with gene-specific long-range PCR.

Front: What does MAPQ 0 mean in BWA output?
Back: The read aligns equally well to two or more locations, so placement is ambiguous.
The first complete, gapless human genome assembly (2022), including centromeres and acrocentric p arms.
No-alt: ALT loci removed so reads don't split MAPQ. Alt-aware: ALTs kept, with an .alt file so BWA handles them correctly.

Front: Three ways liftover between builds can go wrong?
Back: The region is absent in the new build; the REF base differs between builds; strand flips or duplicated regions map ambiguously.

Front: SNV vs MNV vs indel vs SV (size conventions)?
Back: SNV: 1 bp substitution. MNV: adjacent bases changed in one event. Indel: 1–49 bp insertion/deletion. SV: ≥50 bp (a detection convention, not biology).
C>A, C>G, C>T, T>A, T>C, T>G — each also covers its reverse complement (e.g. C>T = G>A).

Front: Why is C>T at CpG so common?
Back: Methylated cytosine at CpG can spontaneously deaminate to thymine; this happens steadily with time, like a molecular clock.

Front: What mutational process produces CC>TT doublets?
Back: UV light, which links adjacent pyrimidines; typical of sun-exposed skin cancers.

Front: Expected Ti/Tv for germline WGS calls?
Back: About 2.0–2.1 (higher, ~3, in exomes). Much lower suggests artifacts.
Missense: one amino acid swapped. Nonsense: codon becomes a stop. Frameshift: indel not a multiple of 3 shifts the reading frame.
mRNA surveillance that destroys transcripts with a premature stop more than ~50–55 nt upstream of the last exon–exon junction.

Front: When does a nonsense variant escape NMD?
Back: When the premature stop is in the last exon or within ~50–55 nt of the last exon–exon junction; a truncated protein may then be made.
Contact (e.g. R248, R273): residues that touch DNA directly. Structural (e.g. R175H): misfold the DNA-binding domain.

Front: Why are TP53 mutations mostly missense?
Back: p53 is a tetramer, so mutant subunits act dominant-negatively; some also gain new functions.
A neomorphic missense change: the enzyme gains a new activity, producing the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate.
Oncogene if >20% of mutations are recurrent missense; tumour suppressor if >20% are inactivating/truncating (Vogelstein 2013).

Front: Oncogene vs tumour suppressor mutation patterns?
Back: Oncogenes: recurrent hotspots, in-frame indels, amplifications, fusions. TSGs: truncations, splice variants and deletions scattered across the gene.
Intron +1/+2 (GT donor) and −1/−2 (AG acceptor). Variants there usually cause exon skipping or cryptic site use.
Skipping removes the CBL docking site, so MET isn't tagged for degradation and accumulates as an active kinase.

Front: Gain vs amplification vs deep deletion?
Back: Gain: a few extra copies. Amplification: many focal copies (e.g. ERBB2). Deep deletion: both copies lost (e.g. CDKN2A).

Front: What is copy-neutral LOH and how is it detected?
Back: Two copies, both from one parent; depth is unchanged, so only B-allele frequency at het SNPs reveals it.
Extrachromosomal circular DNA carrying amplified oncogenes; segregates unevenly, letting copy number change fast (active research).

Front: NAHR vs NHEJ/MMEJ at SV breakpoints?
Back: NAHR: recombination between similar repeats (breakpoints in segdups). NHEJ/MMEJ: direct joining of ends with no or short microhomology.
Discordant pairs (odd insert size/orientation or mates on another chromosome), split reads (soft clips + SA tag), depth changes.
1) Kinase fusion with a dimerising 5′ partner → constitutive kinase (BCR::ABL1, EML4::ALK). 2) Promoter/enhancer swap → oncogene overexpression (TMPRSS2::ERG, IGH::MYC).

Front: Why does RNA help confirm fusions?
Back: Genomic breakpoints are usually intronic; RNA shows the exon–exon junction and whether the transcript is in frame and expressed.
HGVS shifts ambiguous indels to the most 3′ position of the transcript; VCF left-aligns on the + strand. They agree for − strand genes.

Front: What do parentheses in p.(Gly12Asp) mean?
Back: The protein change is predicted from DNA/RNA, not experimentally observed.
In-frame deletion of ELREA (746–750) holds the αC-helix 'on', activating EGFR without ligand; typically TKI-sensitive.
Germline: present from the zygote, in every cell, heritable. Somatic: arose after the zygote, in one cell's clone, not inherited.
A germline variant new in the child, arising in a parental egg or sperm; in all the child's cells but absent from both parents.
A post-zygotic variant arising in early development, present in a subset of cells, possibly across several tissues.

Front: Germline vs somatic variant counts per genome?
Back: Germline: ~4–5 million differences from the reference. Somatic in a tumour: usually thousands to hundreds of thousands — germline outnumbers somatic ~100–1,000×.

Front: Expected VAF of a clonal somatic het mutation (diploid region)?
Back: About purity ÷ 2 (e.g. 0.30 at 60% purity); absent from the normal.

Front: Germline het + LOH in the tumour: VAF pattern?
Back: Normal ~0.5; tumour pushed towards 1 (ALT kept) or 0 (ALT lost), depending on purity.

Front: What is a matched normal for?
Back: Removing the patient's own germline variants (including rare ones) and patient-specific noise, leaving tumour-specific mutations.

Front: Main role of a panel of normals?
Back: Flag recurrent technical artifacts seen across many unrelated normals processed with the same pipeline (FILTER panel_of_normals).

Front: Role of the germline resource (e.g. gnomAD) in Mutect2?
Back: Population allele frequencies act as prior evidence that an allele is germline (FILTER germline).
ALT-supporting reads were seen in the matched normal, arguing against a tumour-specific call.
Clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential: an age-related blood clone with a leukaemia-associated mutation (VAF ≥2%) without blood cancer.
DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1; PPM1D and TP53 enriched after chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

Front: Why is CHIP a problem for tumour-only and cfDNA testing?
Back: Most cfDNA and many sample leukocytes come from blood, so CHIP mutations look like tumour 'somatic' calls.
Tumour cells/DNA in the normal sample; true somatic mutations show small proportional normal VAFs and get filtered (false negatives).

Front: Why is blood a poor normal in blood cancers?
Back: The cancer cells circulate in the blood, so the 'normal' contains tumour DNA. Use skin fibroblasts, nails or sorted non-tumour cells.
A rare germline variant called somatic because the normal had low coverage and the allele is missing from population databases.

Front: How does ancestry affect somatic calling?
Back: Under-represented ancestries have more rare variants missing from gnomAD, raising germline leakage risk.
Many low-VAF 'somatic' calls at common germline SNP sites; quantified by GetPileupSummaries + CalculateContamination.

Front: Do normal tissues carry somatic driver mutations?
Back: Yes. With age, normal tissues (e.g. oesophagus, skin, blood) fill with clones carrying cancer-gene mutations — a driver alone isn't cancer.
Germline heterozygous — possible Li-Fraumeni syndrome; follow the germline-findings policy, not silent filtering.
Likely somatic with tumour-in-normal contamination; check the normal source and estimate TiN before discarding.
Likely a CHIP clone in blood (enriched after chemotherapy), not tumour-derived.

Front: Why is tumour–normal sequencing also a germline test?
Back: The normal genome reveals inherited predisposition variants (e.g. BRCA1/2, Lynch genes, TP53) affecting the patient and relatives.

Front: Steps before returning an incidental germline finding?
Back: Check consent and lab policy, confirm in an accredited clinical test, refer to genetic counselling, verify sample identity.
An inherited cancer-predisposition syndrome caused by germline pathogenic TP53 variants, with very high lifetime cancer risk.
DNA damage or a replication error that escaped repair and was fixed in place by replication.
C>T at CpG (T:G mismatch); a steady, clock-like process (SBS1).
It pairs with A, giving G>T (C>A); BER enzymes OGG1 and MUTYH normally prevent this (SBS18; SBS36 with MUTYH loss).
APOBEC3A/3B deaminate C in single-stranded DNA at TCW motifs → C>T and C>G, often clustered (kataegis); SBS2 and SBS13.
C>T at dipyrimidines and CC>TT doublets from pyrimidine dimers (SBS7a/b, DBS1).
C>A from bulky guanine adducts (e.g. benzo[a]pyrene), with transcriptional strand bias (SBS4).

Front: What does MGMT do, and why does it matter in GBM?
Back: Directly removes O6-methylguanine. MGMT promoter methylation silences it and predicts better temozolomide response.
Single damaged bases (8-oxoG, uracil, small alkylations) and single-strand breaks; uses glycosylases, APE1, POLB, PARP1.
Bulky helix-distorting lesions (UV dimers, tobacco adducts). Defective in xeroderma pigmentosum.
MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 (EPCAM deletions silence MSH2); fix mismatches and slippage loops after replication.
Repairs double-strand breaks in S/G2 using the sister chromatid as an accurate template; BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, RAD51.
NHEJ: directly ligates broken ends (Ku, DNA-PKcs, LIG4), any cell-cycle phase. MMEJ: back-up joining using microhomology via Pol θ (POLQ), leaving microhomology deletions.
Caretakers (repair genes) raise the mutation rate when lost; gatekeepers (APC, RB1) directly control proliferation.
MSI: many ±1 bp indels in microsatellites, hypermutation, MMR SBS signatures (6/15/26/44) and ID1/ID2.

Front: Most common cause of MSI in colorectal cancer?
Back: Sporadic MLH1 promoter hypermethylation, often with BRAF V600E; Lynch syndrome is a minority.
Loss of proofreading → ultramutation (often >100 mut/Mb) with C>A at TCT and C>T at TCG, usually MSS (SBS10a/b).
Microhomology deletions (ID6), SBS3, large-scale LOH/allelic-imbalance scars; small tandem duplications with BRCA1 loss.
Trapped PARP → collapsed forks → double-strand breaks that HR-deficient (BRCA) cells can't repair → death; normal cells survive.
A second mutation restoring the reading frame of a mutant BRCA1/2, restoring HR → PARPi/platinum resistance.

Front: Why are IGH translocations common in B-cell cancers?
Back: B cells deliberately break and mutate antibody genes (V(D)J recombination, class switching, AID); errors join IGH to oncogenes.
Low-VAF C>T (G>A) across many contexts from formalin-induced cytosine deamination; UDG treatment reduces it.
Low-VAF G>T (C>A) from 8-oxoG created during shearing, with read-orientation bias.
Strand bias: ALT only on reads aligned to one reference strand. Orientation bias: ALT only in one F1R2/F2R1 class — damage on one original strand.
Mutect2 --f1r2-tar-gz → LearnReadOrientationModel → FilterMutectCalls --ob-priors; failing calls get FILTER orientation.

Front: Three hypermutated CRCs: how to tell MMR loss from POLE?
Back: MMR loss: many homopolymer indels (MSI-H). POLE: extreme SNV burden with few indels (MSS) and TCT/TCG contexts.
Self-sufficiency in growth signals; insensitivity to anti-growth signals; evading apoptosis; limitless replicative potential; sustained angiogenesis; tissue invasion and metastasis.
Emerging hallmarks: reprogramming energy metabolism; avoiding immune destruction. Enabling characteristics: genome instability and mutation; tumour-promoting inflammation.
Proto-oncogene: normal growth-promoting gene. Oncogene: its gain-of-function, cancer-causing form.
Oncogenes usually need one activated copy (dominant in the cell); TSGs usually need both copies lost (two hits).
Losing one copy of a gene is enough to have an effect; some TSGs (e.g. PTEN) are dose-sensitive.
A tumour's dependence on one activated oncogene, so blocking it causes strong responses (BCR::ABL1, EGFR, ALK).
RTK (EGFR etc.) → RAS → RAF (BRAF) → MEK → ERK → proliferation genes.
A RAS-GAP that switches RAS off; its loss keeps RAS active (tumour suppressor).
PI3K (PIK3CA) makes PIP3 to activate AKT/mTOR; PTEN removes the phosphate to switch it off. PIK3CA gain or PTEN loss both activate the pathway.
Cyclin D–CDK4/6 phosphorylates Rb, releasing E2F to start S phase; p16 (CDKN2A) inhibits CDK4/6.

Front: Why does RB1 loss predict CDK4/6 inhibitor resistance?
Back: CDK4/6 inhibitors work by keeping Rb unphosphorylated and active; without Rb there is nothing to hold E2F.
p16INK4a (inhibits CDK4/6 → Rb pathway) and p14ARF (inhibits MDM2 → p53 pathway), from different first exons and reading frames.
Cell-cycle arrest (via p21), apoptosis (PUMA, BAX) or senescence; normally kept low by MDM2.
TP53 mutation, MDM2 amplification, CDKN2A/ARF loss, viral proteins (HPV E6).
Anti-apoptotic protein overexpressed via t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma; inhibited by venetoclax (CLL, AML).
Hereditary retinoblastoma is bilateral and earlier; sporadic is unilateral and later → two hits needed; gene = RB1 (13q14).
Second mutation, deletion, chromosome/arm loss, mitotic recombination (copy-neutral LOH), promoter methylation.

Front: Which second-hit mechanism is invisible to WGS?
Back: Promoter methylation (e.g. MLH1, CDKN2A); needs methylation assays or RNA expression.

Front: TSG mutation VAF clue for LOH?
Back: A heterozygous-looking TSG mutation with VAF well above purity/2 suggests the wild-type allele was lost.
Driver: gives a selective growth advantage. Passenger: present in the expanding cell but neutral. Most mutations are passengers.

Front: How many drivers in a typical solid tumour?
Back: Roughly two to eight (Vogelstein et al. 2013).
Recurrence above background, dN/dS > 1, hotspot or truncation patterns, functional data, curated databases (Cancer Gene Census, OncoKB).
Genes whose mutations rarely co-occur often act in the same pathway (e.g. KRAS/BRAF; TP53/MDM2).
Glutamate mimics activation-segment phosphorylation → constitutive, RAS-independent monomeric kinase (class I).

Front: BRAF V600E in naevi teaches what?
Back: Oncogene-induced senescence: a strong driver alone doesn't make cancer; further hits (e.g. CDKN2A loss) are needed.
